messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame had been healthy and fiercely independent for most of his adult life, so when he began to notice vague abdominal discomfort and fatigue at 68, he initially dismissed it as something ordinary, the kind of nuisance that could be brushed aside and worked through. He was a widower and lived alone in a quiet house he had shared for decades with his wife, and his days were structured around his work as a policy analyst, where he prided himself on precision, long attention spans, and an ability to sit with complex information for hours. The life-threatening illness entered that ordered life abruptly and without warning. What began as medical appointments quickly escalated into a frightening period of tests, urgent discussions, and the constant sense that his body was no longer behaving in a dependable way. He remembered the worst moments not as a single dramatic event but as a series of terrifying instants in which he felt himself becoming less certain that he would make it through. In retrospect, he could point to the hospital corridors, the clipped voices, the feeling of waiting for results with his mind locked on the possibility of death, as the point at which his body became associated with danger.

After the illness, he returned home physically altered in ways that made him feel exposed in his own house. He described himself as being on guard even inside his own home, as if the quiet rooms might still conceal bad news. He found that his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, his shoulders rigid at the dinner table, his chest tight when the phone rang, his muscles braced without him deciding to do so. This state followed him into ordinary routines. At work, where he had once been able to read policy briefs for long stretches, he now found concentration difficult; he would start a paragraph, lose the thread, and have to go back again and again, frustrated by the way his mind slipped away from him. He noticed the difficulty most when he was preparing reports in his office or reviewing documents at home in the evenings, when he would realize he had been staring at a page without taking anything in. The changes were subtle enough that colleagues might not have noticed, but to Kwame they were evidence that something fundamental had shifted in him.

The memories of the illness came back in a way that startled him. At times he could recall what happened, but feel completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. At other moments the memory did not feel finished or safely in the past; it felt as though it were happening right then, in the same room, with the same terror pressing in on him. When that happened, he would have to stop whatever he was doing. A medical appointment, the smell of antiseptic, or even a random moment alone in the kitchen could bring the whole sequence back with such force that he became overwhelmed by emotion and had to sit down until it passed. He did not describe these episodes in dramatic language; instead, he spoke with visible effort, as if the recollection itself demanded too much from him. The memory could arrive with a flat, distant numbness one moment and then become immediate and engulfing the next, leaving him unable to continue speaking.

Kwame had also come to interpret his bodily reactions with deep distrust. He was certain that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and that this made it impossible for him to feel secure. He said he could no longer trust his own body, because it seemed to tense, alarm, and misfire without warning. What troubled him most was not only the physical unease itself but the meaning he had attached to it: he believed he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the illness had taken something essential from his capacity to respond like himself. That belief was especially painful for a man who had spent his life relying on composure, self-control, and clear judgment. Since the illness, he had found himself living more narrowly, avoiding situations that left him too exposed to reminders of medical vulnerability, and his social world had become smaller and more cautious. The solitude of the house that he once handled easily now sometimes felt amplifying, making every bodily sensation more noticeable and every unexplained pang harder to dismiss.

By the time he sought help, the distress had become impossible to ignore. He came because he was tired of feeling permanently braced, tired of losing his concentration at work, and frightened by how powerfully the memories could seize him months after the illness had passed. More than anything, he wanted to know whether his mind and body could ever feel trustworthy again. He was not asking for a return to the man he had been before in any abstract sense; he was hoping for relief from the constant sense that danger was still near, and for the possibility that he might once again feel something ordinary and human without fear that it would vanish.
